name: Hairstyle simulators / AI haircut preview

lead: Hairstyle simulators place a chosen cut or colour on a photo of your face, and AI versions generate the style rather than overlaying a template. People use them to find a cut that suits their face shape before sitting in a barber's chair.

The chain: upload a selfie, see several styles on your own face, and take the best match to your stylist. The app detects the face and head, then renders the hairstyle. Reference sources say face shape, hair type and head shape affect real-world results. No studies have tested how closely previews match the finished cut.

paras: Users upload a front-facing photo, cycle through cuts and colours, save favourites and show screenshots to their barber or stylist, who adjusts them for the person's actual hair.
Risks are low. Previews may not reflect hair texture, density or growth patterns, and uploading face photos raises privacy concerns.

chain: Pick a style that suits face
angle.text: Users upload a selfie to see a haircut on their own face before visiting a stylist, aiming to choose a cut that suits their face shape. The haircut itself is what changes appearance, and the preview helps pick the right one.

lead: Hairstyle simulators, including AI haircut preview tools, are apps and websites that overlay or generate a hairstyle on a user's photo so they can see a cut or colour on their own face before visiting a stylist. People use them to choose a flattering haircut, to bring a reference image to a barber, and to avoid a style that does not suit their features.

Hair is one of the quickest ways to change how a face looks, and Wikipedia's hairstyle article notes that aesthetic choices may depend on physical attributes such as hair type and face and head shape, alongside desired self-image and the stylist's judgment.[1] Face shape is shaped mainly by the skull's bones, including the maxilla, mandible and zygomatic bones, with soft tissue also contributing.[2]

The tools belong to the wider family of virtual try-on technology, which includes avatars personalised with a customer's face and augmented-reality overlays that track the user on camera.[3] No published study has tested whether previews predict real results.

paras: Users upload or capture a photo and choose from a library of cuts or colours, and AI-based versions generate the style rather than pasting a fixed template.[3] Virtual try-on is also used for clothing, glasses and makeup.

Wikipedia's face article does not offer hairstyle guidance for particular face shapes and presents no evidence for or against such guidance.[2] Popular face-shape rules are common on style websites and forums, but the encyclopedic sources reviewed do not evaluate them; a simulator lets a person test a cut on their own photo rather than rely on a rule.

Virtual try-on methods in general depend on lighting, camera distance and image quality, and no independent accuracy evaluations are described in the reference literature.[3] A preview cannot account for a person's hair texture, density or growth pattern, factors the hairstyle article lists among the physical attributes affecting results.[1] Uploading a face photo to an app also raises privacy questions.

Proponents say a preview helps people pick a cut that suits their features and reduces the risk of an unwanted haircut, and some use it to show a barber a reference. Others in these communities say previews look more flattering than real results. No research has compared previews with outcomes.
